title: From Disparate Knowledge to Unified Fluency Freedom: Generalising the Ratio Table (Part 1)
author: Jon Fant
summary: Jon Fant continues his series on teaching unit conversion by testing whether the Ratio Table scaffold he previously introduced for simple linear conversions (e.g., metres to centimetres) can generalise to the more complex cases of area and volume conversion. He walks through worked examples showing that converting units of area requires squaring the underlying linear ratio (because area involves two dimensions) and converting units of volume requires cubing it (because volume involves three), and demonstrates step by step how the same ratio-table structure -- fill in the known linear fact, apply the appropriate power, then scale horizontally or vertically to find the answer -- handles both cases cleanly. His broader pedagogical argument is that students typically experience unit conversion, area/volume scale factors, and similar-shapes problems as disconnected topics each requiring a memorised rule, when in fact all of them derive from the same proportional structure across L, L², and L³. By making that structure explicit and visible in a single reusable scaffold, Fant argues, students gain a model that survives even when a specific memorised fact fades, since it can be reconstructed from the underlying relationship. The piece closes by previewing a follow-up article applying the same ratio-table logic directly to similar-shapes problems.
points: Central thesis: unit conversion, area/volume scale factors, and similar shapes are not separate topics requiring separate memorised rules -- they all derive from the same proportional relationship (L, L², L³) and can be taught through one reusable scaffold.

Demonstrates that converting area units requires squaring the base linear ratio and converting volume units requires cubing it, with the Ratio Table making that operation explicit and visible rather than an opaque memorised multiplier.

Frames the pedagogical advantage as resilience: a scaffold built from a connected structural fact gives students a fallback method when a specific memorised conversion factor fades, versus a bare fact with no way to reconstruct it.
Uses side-by-side worked examples (5.2 m² to cm², 0.45 m³ to cm³) to show the identical three-step ratio-table process applies regardless of dimensional complexity.
Sets up a Part 2 extending the same framework to similar-shapes problems, positioning the ratio table as a unifying model across a cluster of GCSE-level topics.
quotes: [1] "Unit conversion, similar shapes, scale factors, scale diagrams. In your classroom, do your students see these as a unified set of proportional concepts, or do they hold disparate knowledge? I think too often, the answer is the latter.

[2] "The true test of the ratio table scaffold is its ability to generalise. Does the ratio table only work for simple linear conversions? Or can it successfully manage the complexities of area, volume, and beyond to other work such as similar shapes? So do they generalise, yes they do!
[3] "Because the conversion factor applies to both the length and the width, we must square the underlying linear relationship. The Ratio Table makes this connection explicit and transparent.

[4] "We now see that 1 m 2 = 10,000 cm 2 . This is no longer only a fact to be memorised; it is a relationship derived from the known linear fact. Is it bad to memorise facts? No, but if we have connected knowledge we are more likely to be able to use that knowledge, or fall back to the connection if the factual knowledge starts to fade.

[5] "Volume is measured in cubic units (L 3 ). Following the same logic, if the conversion factor applies across all three dimensions (length, width, and height), we must cube the underlying linear ratio.

[6] "The Ratio Table is not just an alternative method for unit conversion; it is a mathematical framework that reveals the underlying proportional structure across different contexts... This is a consistent, non-negotiable mathematical truth, derived directly from the dimension of the measure.

[7] "By grounding both metric unit conversions and the scale factors for similar shapes in the same principle (the relationship between L, L 2 , and L 3 ), we give our students a single, powerful model to generalise across traditionally separate topics. We replace rote memorisation with structural understanding.
